reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Vascular ectasias are dilated, thin-walled mucosal and submucosal vessels that appear as flat, red, fern-like or punctate lesions and are a common cause of obscure or occult gastrointestinal bleeding

Gastric antral vascular ectasia (watermelon stomach) shows red stripes radiating along the antral folds and is distinct from portal hypertensive gastropathy despite sometimes coexisting with cirrhosis
Most patients present with chronic iron-deficiency anaemia from slow blood loss rather than dramatic haemorrhage
Associations include chronic kidney disease, aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome, via acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency), cirrhosis, and connective tissue disease
Endoscopic ablation, typically with argon plasma coagulation, is the mainstay of treatment and often requires repeated sessions
In Heyde syndrome, correcting the aortic stenosis by valve replacement can resolve the acquired coagulopathy and the bleeding
Refractory antral vascular ectasia may be treated with endoscopic band ligation, and diffuse or hereditary lesions may need iron replacement and, occasionally, systemic pharmacotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Angiodysplasia (vascular ectasia) consists of abnormally dilated, tortuous, thin-walled ectatic vessels within the mucosa and submucosa, thought to arise from chronic, low-grade venous obstruction or degenerative vascular changes that promote the formation of arteriovenous communications. In gastric antral vascular ectasia the dilated capillaries are accompanied by fibromuscular hyperplasia and fibrin thrombi in the antral lamina propria, producing the characteristic red stripes. Because these fragile vessels lie superficially, they bleed slowly and recurrently; in Heyde syndrome, high shear across a stenotic aortic valve degrades large von Willebrand factor multimers, adding an acquired bleeding tendency that amplifies blood loss from the ectasias.
additionalDifferentials: Peptic ulcer disease or erosive gastropathy
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to identify and characterise the ectasias and distinguish antral vascular ectasia from portal hypertensive gastropathy
Full blood count and iron studies to quantify chronic blood loss
Echocardiography to detect aortic stenosis where Heyde syndrome is suspected
Assessment of renal function and screening for associated connective tissue disease
Testing for acquired von Willebrand factor deficiency in the appropriate context
Capsule endoscopy or device-assisted enteroscopy when small-bowel angiodysplasia is suspected
redFlags: Transfusion-dependent or recurrent bleeding despite endoscopic therapy
New aortic stenosis with unexplained gastrointestinal bleeding suggesting Heyde syndrome
reference.prognosis: The condition tends to be chronic and recurrent, and although endoscopic ablation controls bleeding in many patients, repeat treatments are frequently needed; in Heyde syndrome, valve replacement can be curative, whereas diffuse or hereditary lesions carry a higher risk of ongoing transfusion dependence.
pitfalls: Confusing antral vascular ectasia with portal hypertensive gastropathy and applying portal-pressure-lowering therapy that does not help
Overlooking coexisting aortic stenosis and the opportunity to correct Heyde syndrome
Attributing iron-deficiency anaemia to diet or menstruation and missing occult vascular lesions
Assuming a single ablation session will be definitive
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
